input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-464: Xtreme Theory. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: A fast paced, informal look at current trends in the theory of computing. Each week is dedicated to a different topic and will explore some of the underlying theory as well as the practical applications of the theory. Sample topics may include: quantum cryptography, networks and complex systems, social welfare and game theory, zero knowledge protocols. Students will be evaluated on homework assignments and a final presentation. Offered every other year. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

Source excerpts:

[nist-cryptographic-standards]
Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.

[nist-ssdf]
The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.

[rit-csci-464]
A fast paced, informal look at current trends in the theory of computing. Each week is dedicated to a different topic and will explore some of the underlying theory as well as the practical applications of the theory. Sample topics may include: quantum cryptography, networks and complex systems, social welfare and game theory, zero knowledge protocols. Students will be evaluated on homework assignments and a final presentation. Offered every other year. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

beats.claim: Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters.
beats.example: The NIST FIPS 180-4 standard specifies AES-256 as an approved algorithm for encryption.
beats.title: Introduction to Cryptographic Standards
beats.visualDirection: Display a table comparing AES-128, AES-256, and ChaCha20 with their approved parameter sets.

beats.claim: Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly.
beats.example: Using AES in CBC mode with a 256-bit key ensures that plaintext data remains unreadable without the decryption key.
beats.title: Encryption and Confidentiality
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart illustrating key generation, encryption process, and decryption process with labeled security checks.

beats.claim: Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways.
beats.example: A digital signature uses a private key to sign a message, while a message authentication code uses a shared secret to verify integrity.
beats.title: Message Authentication and Digital Signatures
beats.visualDirection: Create a side-by-side diagram showing how a digital signature verifies sender authenticity versus how HMAC verifies message integrity.

beats.claim: Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters.
beats.example: Cryptographically secure random number generators produce unpredictable values for session keys and nonces to prevent replay attacks.
beats.title: Random Number Generation
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a sequence of random numbers generated by a CSPRNG versus a pseudo-random number generator, highlighting unpredictability.

beats.claim: Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction.
beats.example: A key management system automatically rotates encryption keys every 90 days and securely destroys old keys from memory and storage.
beats.title: Key Management Practices
beats.visualDirection: Draw a lifecycle diagram showing each stage of key management with icons for generation, distribution, storage, rotation, revocation, and destruction.

beats.claim: Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block.
beats.example: In GCM mode, the encryption primitive processes data in blocks while simultaneously computing an authentication tag for integrity.
beats.title: Modes of Operation
beats.visualDirection: Show a block diagram of a cipher operating in GCM mode, highlighting block processing and authentication tag generation.

beats.claim: Validation checks implementations against specified requirements.
beats.example: FIPS validation ensures that a software implementation of AES matches the mathematical specifications and passes test vectors.
beats.title: Implementation Validation
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist of validation criteria including test vectors, side-channel resistance, and compliance with FIPS requirements.

beats.claim: The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups.
beats.example: The SSDF framework organizes security practices into Prepare, Protect, Produce, and Respond groups to guide secure development.
beats.title: Secure Software Development Framework
beats.visualDirection: Create a four-quadrant matrix labeled Prepare, Protect, Produce, and Respond, with each quadrant containing key practices.

beats.claim: Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development.
beats.example: Training developers in secure coding standards and providing access to secure development tools establishes the foundation for secure practices.
beats.title: Prepare the Organization
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart connecting people training, process documentation, and technology provisioning to secure development readiness.

beats.claim: Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts.
beats.example: Access control policies and code repository permissions ensure that only authorized developers can view or modify source code.
beats.title: Protect the Software
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a network diagram showing code repositories, access controls, and authentication mechanisms protecting development artifacts.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of cryptographic standards and their roles in ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity.
Explain the four practice groups of the Secure Software Development Framework and their responsibilities in secure development.
Apply practical analysis methods to evaluate cryptographic implementations and software security practices against established standards.
